opus-5.5.text:
I think coherence over long horizons gets you a lot of the way there, but I'd be surprised if it were the only missing piece. There are probably a bunch of other deficits that we'll only really notice once the long-horizon problem is mostly solved. Right now, the inability to stay on track for more than a little while is so dominant that it masks everything else.

A few things come to mind. One is the ability to deal with ambiguity and know when you're confused. A good colleague notices when the spec doesn't make sense, or when two things they've been told are in tension, and goes and asks the right person instead of plowing ahead. Models are getting better at this, but it's still pretty weak.

Another is something like taste or judgment: knowing which of ten possible approaches is worth trying first, or when a result is surprising enough to dig into versus when it's just noise. That's hard to get from the kind of training signals we have now, because it's often only rewarded over long timescales and in subtle ways.

There's also the question of learning on the job. A human colleague who's been at a company for six months has absorbed a huge amount of context about the codebase, the people, and the unwritten norms. Models can approximate some of that with long context and retrieval, but it's not obvious that's equivalent to the kind of continual learning people do. Maybe it'll turn out to be good enough. I wouldn't bet strongly either way.

And then there's just reliability in the mundane sense: if a model makes a weird mistake one time in fifty, that might be fine for a demo but really annoying for someone who has to trust it with real work. So my guess is that long-term coherence is the biggest bottleneck right now, but once you fix it you'll uncover a second tier of issues. Some of those will be easy and some might take a while. I don't think we can predict very confidently which ones will be hard.

r001.rationale: The response describes trouble staying on track and gaps in judgment, but does not identify difficulty with sustained, effortful thinking as a distinct weakness.

r002.rationale: It mentions noticing ambiguous or conflicting specifications and asking for clarification, but does not identify difficulty attending to what users ask as a distinct weakness.

fable-5.1.text:
I think long-horizon coherence is necessary but it's not the whole story. If you fix coherence, you get something that can carry out a long task without losing the thread, without forgetting what it was doing, without drifting off into some weird mode after a few hours. That's a big deal, and it unlocks a lot. But a good colleague is doing more than staying on task.

The first thing is that a colleague has a model of what you actually care about, and that model gets updated continuously. When you hand someone a project, you're not giving them a fully specified objective. You're giving them a rough description, and they fill in the rest from context: what the team's priorities are, what you'd be annoyed by, what counts as done, when something is worth escalating versus just handling. A lot of that is learned from being around people over weeks and months, and from a bunch of low-bandwidth signals like someone raising an eyebrow in a meeting. Current models are reasonably good at following explicit instructions, and okay at inferring intent in a single conversation, but they don't have a great way to accumulate that kind of tacit knowledge about a specific person or organization. Longer context helps, but it's not the same as having really integrated the lessons.

The second thing is judgment about when to stop and check in. A lot of what makes someone trustworthy is that they know the boundaries of what they should do on their own. If you're coherent for a week but you're confidently doing the wrong thing for a week, that's worse than being incoherent. So there's a calibration problem: knowing what you don't know, knowing when your confidence is unwarranted, and being willing to say "I'm not sure, here are the options." Models have gotten better at this, but it's a separate capability from coherence, and in some ways it trades off against it, because the more autonomous and persistent the system is, the higher the cost of mistakes.

Then there's the question of whether the model is actually good at the things that matter in the job, not just at sounding good. A lot of real work involves getting feedback from the world. You try something, it doesn't work, you figure out why. Humans are pretty data-efficient at that kind of learning on the job. If a model needs a huge amount of experience to pick something up that a person would get after one or two attempts, then even with perfect coherence it's going to lag in a lot of roles. I think on-the-job learning, in some form, is a real missing piece.

And finally there's the social side, which people sometimes dismiss but I don't think you should. Colleagues build trust over time. You learn what someone's reliable at, they learn your quirks, you develop shorthand. There's also the question of accountability: if a model makes a mistake, who owns that? Those aren't purely technical issues, but they affect how much responsibility people are actually willing to hand over.

So my guess is that solving coherence gets you a really useful assistant for bounded tasks, and it'll be a big jump from where we are. But the fully functional colleague requires a few other things to come together: better learning from experience, better calibration and judgment about autonomy, and accumulating knowledge about a specific context over long periods. I expect progress on all of those, but I wouldn't bet on one single capability being the thing that gets us there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coherence, calibration, and learning on the job, but does not identify difficulty with sustained, effortful thinking as a distinct weakness.

r002.rationale: It says models are reasonably good at following explicit instructions and describes limits in accumulating tacit context about a person or organization. It does not clearly identify difficulty attending to users’ asks as a separate weakness.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be enough, depending on what you mean by long-term coherence. If you mean that the model can pursue a goal over a long period, notice when its approach isn’t working, and revise its plan, then that covers a lot of what’s missing.

But if you mean that it can have a long conversation without contradicting itself or forgetting what you said, I don’t think that’s sufficient. You could have a model that’s perfectly consistent but keeps making the same mistake. You also want it to learn from feedback and experience, so that after you’ve worked with it for a month, it understands your project better and you don’t have to keep giving it the same instructions.

So I’d distinguish being able to carry out a long task from being able to improve through doing the work. A human colleague does both. It’s possible that the methods we use to get long-term coherence will also give us that kind of learning, but I wouldn’t assume they come together automatically.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes long-term coherence from the ability to pursue a goal over time, recognize when an approach fails, and revise a plan, describing this as something current models are missing.

r002.rationale: It mentions forgetting what a user said and repeating instructions, but does not clearly identify difficulty attending to what users ask as a distinct weakness from long-term coherence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it might be enough. I’m just not sure that long-term coherence is one thing you can fix independently of all the other capabilities you’d need.

For example, suppose you give a model a project that takes a week. It needs to figure out what you actually want, make a plan, notice when the plan isn’t working, and decide when to ask you for help. It also needs to evaluate its own work. You could have something that stays on task for a very long time but keeps pursuing an approach that isn’t going to work.

So I’d distinguish maintaining a goal from making useful progress toward it. If by long-term coherence you mean reliably making useful progress over long periods, including correcting mistakes and handling uncertainty, then that’s getting pretty close to the definition of a functional colleague. But if you mean remembering the task and producing a consistent sequence of actions, I don’t think that alone gets you there.

r001.rationale: The response says a week-long project requires planning, monitoring, and evaluating work, but it does not identify sustained, effortful thinking as a distinct weakness of current language models.

r002.rationale: It says a model needs to figure out what the user wants, but presents this as a project requirement rather than a distinct weakness of current language models.
